hints: Think about where a normal heartbeat starts. Which small patch of tissue in the right atrium wall generates excitation spontaneously without nerves?
Once that excitation starts, how must it travel so both atria contract together as one unit to push blood into the ventricles?
walkthrough:
Start with the pacemaker - the SAN**
The SAN is a group of specialised muscle cells in the wall of the right atrium. It is myogenic, meaning it can generate its own rhythmic wave of excitation without needing a nerve impulse first. That is what sets the heart rate and initiates each beat.

Spread across the atria to cause systole**
The wave of excitation spreads quickly from cell to cell across both atrial walls. This causes the cardiac muscle in the atria to contract together, which is atrial systole, forcing blood down into the ventricles.
Final answer: The SAN sends out a wave of excitation / electrical impulses, which spreads across the atrial walls causing atrial systole.

hints: If excitation spread directly from atria muscle to ventricle muscle, everything would contract at once. What structural barrier prevents this direct spread?
Think about the only route left for excitation to reach the ventricles and why a short pause there is useful for filling.
walkthrough:
Block direct spread with insulating tissue**
There is a layer of non-conducting fibrous tissue between the atrial walls and the ventricular walls. This means the wave of excitation from the SAN cannot pass straight down into the ventricles.

Force a detour with a delay at the AVN**
The only conducting route is through the AVN in the septum, then down the bundle of His and Purkyne tissue. The AVN delays the impulse briefly. That delay gives time for the atria to finish contracting and empty blood into the ventricles, so atria contract first, then ventricles.

Final answer: Non-conducting fibres between atria and ventricles prevent direct spread, so excitation must pass via the AVN down the septum. The AVN delays the impulse by ~0.1 s, allowing the atria to complete contraction and empty before ventricles contract.

hints: Remember valves only respond to pressure difference. A valve opens when pressure behind it is higher and closes when pressure in front is higher. Look at which two lines cross at each point E, F, G, H.
Points E and H involve left atrium vs left ventricle, so they must be the atrioventricular valve. Points F and G involve left ventricle vs aorta, so they must be the semilunar valve.

At E ventricle pressure just rises above atrium, and at F ventricle just rises above aorta. At G ventricle just falls below aorta, and at H ventricle just falls below atrium. Decide open or close for each.
walkthrough:
Identify which valve from which lines cross**
E and H are where the left ventricle and left atrium pressure lines cross, so they involve the valve between them: the bicuspid or left atrioventricular valve. F and G are where the left ventricle and aorta lines cross, so they involve the valve between them: the semilunar or aortic valve.

Use rising vs falling ventricle pressure**
At E, ventricular pressure rises just above atrial pressure during ventricular systole, so the bicuspid valve is pushed shut to prevent backflow. At F, ventricular pressure rises just above aortic pressure, so the semilunar valve is pushed open to allow ejection into the aorta.

Finish the cycle on the falling side**
At G, ventricular pressure falls just below aortic pressure during diastole, so the semilunar valve closes. At H, ventricular pressure falls just below atrial pressure, so the bicuspid valve opens to allow ventricular filling.
Final answer: E - bicuspid / left atrioventricular valve closes; F - semilunar / aortic valve opens; G - semilunar / aortic valve closes; H - bicuspid / left atrioventricular valve opens.

hints: Compare the peak heights of the left ventricle curve and the left atrium curve in Fig. 2.1. Which chamber reaches a much higher pressure when it contracts?
Link higher pressure generation to structure. Which chamber needs thicker wall and more cardiac muscle to pump blood further, and what values prove it?
walkthrough:
Read the pressure difference as evidence of force**
In Fig. 2.1 the left ventricle pressure rises to about $15 \text{ kPa}$ during systole, while the left atrium pressure stays very low at about $0$ to $1 \text{ kPa}$. Higher pressure means a more forceful contraction.

Link pressure to wall thickness**
Pressure is generated by cardiac muscle contraction. The left ventricle has a much thicker wall with more muscle because it must pump blood around the whole body via the aorta, while the left atrium only pumps a short distance into the ventricle. So the graph proves the ventricle wall is thicker.

Final answer: Left ventricle generates much higher pressure than left atrium on contraction because its wall is thicker with more cardiac muscle. E.g. ventricle peaks at ~15 kPa while atrium stays at ~1 kPa.
